title: Explainers for every id in the portal
summary: Each id the portal shows opens a popup with these words: what it is, its status and what it links to.

refs.title: P0 Planning
refs.summary: Goal: Plan written, checked and approved by you; no app code yet. Build the project's memory (the wiki) and a plan portal for you, before any Ferrum code. You walked through the portal, answered the first two rounds of questions, approved 30 pages and signed off planning on 11 Oct, after the final check passed.

refs.title: P1 Foundation
refs.summary: Goal: Tools confirmed, empty project builds, riskiest ideas tested. Confirm the installed tools, set up an empty Rust project with automatic checks, and test the four riskiest technical assumptions with throwaway experiments before the real app is designed. You gave the go on 11 Oct.

refs.title: P2 First working app
refs.summary: Goal: One window browses websites safely: address bar, back, forward, refresh. Build the first real Ferrum: a trusted shell around one website view, with safe navigation and a locked bridge so websites cannot call the app.

refs.title: P3 Tabs and sessions
refs.summary: Goal: Many tabs, restored after a restart, with separate data per site. Turn the single view into tabs: switching, shortcuts, restore after a crash, a profile per site, history, basic downloads, a settings screen and a sidebar.

refs.title: P4 Security
refs.summary: Goal: Blocking, permissions and isolation proven by tests; threat model written. Build the security rules engine and prove with attack-style tests what Ferrum protects and what it does not. The cost of security is only designed here; it is measured in P6.

refs.title: P5 Measurement
refs.summary: Ferrum learns to measure itself: memory, CPU, startup and page-load timing, plus a network log of addresses and timings only. Each meter is checked against helper programs with known usage; a meter that fails blocks P6. Before it starts you answer three privacy questions about the network log.

refs.title: P6 Benchmarks
refs.summary: Build a test bench that compares Ferrum with Chrome, Edge and a bare Tauri app under identical conditions. Check it against itself to learn the noise level, write predictions down in advance, then run the first test campaign. Data is only collected here; it is interpreted in P8.

refs.title: P7 Smart tab sleeping
refs.summary: Ferrum learns to put unused tabs to sleep, and later close them while remembering their place, without ever losing your work. Four strategies (never, fixed timer, memory pressure, cost-aware) run in one app and are compared on the test bench. Similar ideas already exist, so we also finish the literature check.

refs.title: P8 Research paper
refs.summary: Goal: Results analysed; paper drafted with every claim checked. Turn the raw data from the campaigns into analysed results and a draft paper. Every number comes from scripts, every citation is verified, failed experiments are reported, and nothing is called new beyond what you approved. You read the whole paper as its responsible author.

refs.title: P0 task: Save the starting documents
refs.summary: Your brief and scoping answers are the ground truth → store them word for word, never edited → every later page can cite them.

refs.title: P0 task: Create the plan app skeleton
refs.summary: Loose versions break things later → create the web app with exact versions and three small feasibility tests → a stable base for the rest.

refs.title: P0 task: Teach the app to read the wiki
refs.summary: The app shows wiki pages → a reader that checks each page's header against the rules → bad pages are flagged, not shown wrongly.

refs.title: P0 task: Fingerprint pages exactly like the reference
refs.summary: Approvals are tied to page fingerprints → compute them in the app exactly like the reference script → a changed page can never keep an old approval.

refs.title: P0 task: Build the app's views and wiki check
refs.summary: You need to see the plan, not raw files → dashboard, roadmap, architecture, decisions, risks and research views, plus an automatic wiki check → the plan is readable and checked.

refs.title: P0 task: Build the approvals store
refs.summary: Approvals must not be lost or forged → a local-only store with safe writes, every approval state tested → no approval is silently wrong.

refs.title: P0 task: Build the approval screens
refs.summary: Approvals were first planned inside the app → approve, change and reject buttons with an outdated-page badge → later replaced: you now approve in Claude Code.

refs.title: P0 task: Run the full plan-app test gate
refs.summary: Each piece passed on its own → run every check together and save the output → proof the whole app works.

refs.title: P0 task: Portal v2, then your review
refs.summary: You found v1 too technical → rebuild it as a read-only portal in plain words, fed by text Claude writes from the wiki → you review it and approve in Claude Code; Claude records each approval.

refs.title: P0 task: Close P0
refs.summary: All checks pass and the pages are approved → you approve the phase exit in Claude Code → Claude pauses; P1 starts only when you explicitly say go.

refs.title: P0 task: Write five research notes
refs.summary: Plans built from memory go stale → research the wiki method, Tauri and WebView2, measurement, the plan-app stack and related work, with dated sources → decisions rest on checked facts.

refs.title: P0 task: Write the wiki rules and live status
refs.summary: Many sessions and helpers edit the wiki → one rulebook (page shapes, fingerprints) plus a live status file → any session can pick up where the last one stopped.

refs.title: P0 task: Describe the architecture and its parts
refs.summary: The app has many parts with different trust levels → one page per part, saying what it talks to → security boundaries are visible before any code.

refs.title: P0 task: Write the decisions and the risk register
refs.summary: Choices and risks get forgotten → one page per decision (19 at the time; more were added later) and per risk, with likelihood, impact and response → we can always see why, and what could go wrong.

refs.title: P0 task: Write the research plan pages
refs.summary: Ferrum is also a research project → questions, predictions, experiments, metrics and test workloads, linked to each other → nothing is measured without a reason.

refs.title: P0 task: Write phase pages, index and log
refs.summary: Work spans nine phases and many sessions → a page per phase, an index of every page and a running log → you and Claude can find anything.

refs.title: P0 task: Check the whole wiki
refs.summary: Hundreds of linked pages drift → run every rule by hand or script and fingerprint the raw files → work starts from a clean, tamper-evident base.

refs.title: P0 task: Install Node and record versions
refs.summary: The plan app needs Node 24 → install it and record exact versions → builds can be repeated.

refs.title: P1 task: Confirm and record the toolchain
refs.summary: Rust 1.99, the C++ build tools, Node 24 and PowerShell 7 are already installed → confirm each works, record exact versions, add the licence checker → every later result names the tools it was built with.

refs.title: P1 task: Re-confirm the history-based wiki checks
refs.summary: These checks were already built during P0 → P1 re-runs them on the new history and adjusts them only if needed → tampering with raw files or stale dates are still caught; P1 has one less real build task.

refs.title: P1 task: Turn on automatic checks on GitHub
refs.summary: Mistakes are cheaper caught at once → one GitHub workflow and one local script running the same checks → every change is tested the same way.

refs.title: P1 task: Check dependency licences and alerts
refs.summary: Third-party code can carry unsuitable licences or known holes → a licence allowlist and a security-alert check, lock files committed → we only use what we may and should.

refs.title: P1 task: Start the public docs
refs.summary: Readers need security, benchmark and reproducibility notes → short starter files linking to the wiki → documentation grows with the code.

refs.title: P1 task: Start the literature review
refs.summary: A research claim needs prior work → write the search method and read the first batch, with checked sources → no novelty is claimed without evidence.

refs.title: P1 task: Warn when code changes without its page
refs.summary: Code and its wiki page must change together → a check that runs before each commit warns when they don't → the plan never drifts from the code.

refs.title: P1 task: Run the gate; your review
refs.summary: All tasks done → run every check on one commit and save the output → you review the experiment evidence and approve the exit.

refs.title: P1 task: Pin the Tauri and web-tool versions
refs.summary: Generated templates change under us → pin Tauri's command-line tool, Vite and TypeScript exactly, and write the experiments by hand → experiments can be rerun identically.

refs.title: P1 task: Record this computer's hardware
refs.summary: Benchmark numbers depend on the machine → record CPU, memory, graphics, power plan and browser versions → results can be compared and repeated.

refs.title: P1 task: Set ignore rules and licences
refs.summary: Build output and local data must not reach git → ignore rules plus MIT and Apache licence files → a clean, legally clear repo.

refs.title: P1 task: Create the empty Rust workspace
refs.summary: Code needs a home → empty Rust libraries in the planned folders, with a pinned Rust version → every later task has a place to go.

refs.title: P1 task: Experiment 1: several web views in one window
refs.summary: Tauri's multi-view feature is experimental → build a throwaway app with three tab views and test resize, focus, overlap, blank pages and freezes → if it is unstable, the design changes before P2, not after.

refs.title: P1 task: Experiment 2: a separate profile per site
refs.summary: Per-site isolation needs a profile chosen when a view is created, and Tauri does not offer that → try four routes → pick one that keeps cookies apart, before tabs are built.

refs.title: P1 task: Experiment 3: low-level WebView2 calls
refs.summary: Suspend, memory limits and crash events are only reachable below Tauri → call each one through Tauri's escape hatch → we know which lifecycle and security features are possible.

refs.title: P1 task: Experiment 4: test robot drives the app
refs.summary: Benchmarks drive browsers with Playwright through a debugging channel → connect to the experiment app, Chrome and Edge the same way → one fair harness for all.

refs.title: P1 task: Decide the design from the experiments
refs.summary: Four experiment verdicts → update the risks and propose decisions on profiles, back/forward and the benchmark path → you decide, then P2 and P3 are revised to match.

refs.title: P2 task: Build local test pages
refs.summary: Real websites change → a local server with fixed pages (redirects, pop-ups, cookies, slow and error pages) → navigation tests give the same answer every run.

refs.title: P2 task: New windows and outside links
refs.summary: Links open new windows or other apps such as mail → follow the setting, and ask before handing off to another app → nothing launches without your consent.

refs.title: P2 task: Keep cookies across restarts
refs.summary: Logins should survive a restart → keep site data in a fixed local folder → you stay signed in.

refs.title: P2 task: Developer tools only in test builds
refs.summary: Developer tools expose page internals → enable them only in debug builds → the release app stays locked.

refs.title: P2 task: Google sign-in: offer the normal browser
refs.summary: Google may refuse sign-in inside embedded views → detect its sign-in page and offer the system browser, never disguise the app → we respect Google's rules.

refs.title: P2 task: Structured logs, no crashes
refs.summary: Problems need evidence → Machine-readable log lines and clear errors, no crashing on bad navigation → failures can be diagnosed.

refs.title: P2 task: Quick whole-app tests
refs.summary: Features interact → one suite drives shell and website view with Playwright, plus a manual list → one command shows the first milestone works.

refs.title: P2 task: Update docs and part pages
refs.summary: Code changed → README, security notes, known limits and part pages updated with the verified commit → docs match reality.

refs.title: P2 task: Literature batch 2
refs.summary: Research runs alongside code → read on WebView2 and Chromium processes, page lifecycle and embedded-view resource studies → evidence for later experiments.

refs.title: P2 task: Run the gate; your review
refs.summary: All tasks done → run every check and save the output → you try the release build and approve the first milestone.

refs.title: P2 task: Create the desktop app
refs.summary: The design was fixed in P1 → create the app with the chosen Tauri version and hosting route → the shell window opens.

refs.title: P2 task: Lock the bridge to the app
refs.summary: Every web view can reach the app's command channel → grant permissions to the shell only, none to websites → a website cannot control Ferrum.

refs.title: P2 task: Settings model
refs.summary: Start page, navigation rules and data folder must be valid → typed settings with safe defaults → bad settings never crash or weaken the app.

refs.title: P2 task: Clean up address-bar input
refs.summary: People type anything → one tested function turns input into a safe address or refuses it → malformed input never navigates.

refs.title: P2 task: Show a website and track it
refs.summary: The shell must know where the page is → create the website view and report address and loading state → the address bar and spinner are always right.

refs.title: P2 task: Back, forward, refresh
refs.summary: Basic browsing → use the browser's own history calls and grey out buttons that cannot work → behaves like a normal browser.

refs.title: P2 task: Loading and error screens
refs.summary: Pages are slow or fail → spinner and error panel drawn by the shell, never by loading the app's own pages into the website view → clear feedback without weakening security.

refs.title: P2 task: Follow redirects correctly
refs.summary: Sites redirect → show the final address and stop loops with an error → the address bar never lies.

refs.title: P3 task: Tab rules as plain code
refs.summary: Tab logic has many edge cases → write it without the window and test random sequences of actions → exactly one active tab, ids never reused.

refs.title: P3 task: Guard against the freeze bug
refs.summary: Creating views from blocking code freezes on Windows → make that path impossible and test it in a loop → the bug cannot come back.

refs.title: P3 task: One integration suite
refs.summary: Many features → one command runs every P3 test → a single green run proves the milestone.

refs.title: P3 task: Literature batch 3
refs.summary: Tab lifecycle is the core research idea → read tab-usage studies and Chrome and Edge lifecycle policies → prior art for P7.

refs.title: P3 task: Docs, gate, your review
refs.summary: Tabs done → update part pages, known limits and the README, then run the gate → you use Ferrum for a real working session and approve.

refs.title: P3 task: Settings screen
refs.summary: You need to change startup sites, profiles and the download folder → a settings screen in the trusted shell, checked by the app → websites still cannot touch settings.

refs.title: P3 task: Sidebar of tabs and history
refs.summary: Website views are always drawn over the shell → place the sidebar beside them, never on top → nothing is hidden or overlapped.

refs.title: P3 task: One web view per tab
refs.summary: Each tab needs its own view → create views only from non-blocking code, hide and show on switch, release fully on close → no freezes or leftover processes.

refs.title: P3 task: Tab strip and shortcuts
refs.summary: Shortcuts must work even while typing in a website → handle them in the shell without giving websites access → fast and still safe.

refs.title: P3 task: Saved settings and startup sites
refs.summary: Settings must survive crashes and upgrades → a versioned file, written safely, with migration → never lost or half-written.

refs.title: P3 task: Restore tabs after restart or crash
refs.summary: Crashes happen → save the tab list regularly and on exit, safely → after a forced kill you get your tabs back.

refs.title: P3 task: Separate profile per site
refs.summary: Sites should not see each other's data → assign profiles using the route chosen in P1 → cookies stay apart.

refs.title: P3 task: History
refs.summary: You need back/forward per tab and a list of visited pages → kept locally, clearable, never in the repo → useful without leaking.

refs.title: P3 task: Basic downloads
refs.summary: Files must land somewhere sensible → default folder or a prompt, with progress and errors → downloads are visible.

refs.title: P3 task: Shell stays responsive
refs.summary: A busy tab must not freeze the browser → switch tabs and type while another tab burns CPU → the shell stays usable.

refs.title: P4 task: Threat model
refs.summary: Controls need a reason → list what we protect, who attacks and where trust changes, and map each threat to a control and test, or 'not enforced' → every later task traces to a threat.

refs.title: P4 task: Recover from crashes
refs.summary: Page processes crash → show a crashed tab, allow reload, keep the shell alive → one bad site cannot take Ferrum down.

refs.title: P4 task: One security test suite
refs.summary: Your brief lists ten security tests → one suite mapping each to a test, kept apart from speed tests → coverage is visible.

refs.title: P4 task: Design the cost experiments
refs.summary: Security costs time and memory → build small timing tests and finish the experiment designs, claiming no numbers → P6 measures it properly.

refs.title: P4 task: Literature batch 4
refs.summary: The paper needs security context → read site-isolation and embedded-browser security studies → the trade-offs are grounded.

refs.title: P4 task: Gate and your review
refs.summary: Controls are tested → run the gate → you review the threat model and the 'not enforced' list, and approve.

refs.title: P4 task: Selectable isolation modes
refs.summary: Isolation has a cost → three modes set in config (shared, a profile per site, a data folder per site), observed rather than assumed → P6 can compare them.

refs.title: P4 task: Benchmark-only 'no security' switch
refs.summary: Measuring security's cost needs a version without it → a build-time switch for local test pages only, proven absent from release builds → no risk of shipping it.

refs.title: P4 task: Security settings screen
refs.summary: You manage blocked sites and permissions → add them to the settings screen through checked app commands → websites still cannot touch them.

refs.title: P4 task: Rules engine
refs.summary: Navigation needs one decision point → plain Rust rules: block and allow lists, HTTPS upgrade, ask for other link types, deny anything unreadable → safe by default, every decision explained.

refs.title: P4 task: Check every navigation path
refs.summary: Tauri's hook misses unreadable addresses and embedded frames → also hook WebView2's own events and re-check each redirect → no way around the rules by redirect, frame or pop-up.

refs.title: P4 task: Ask before opening other apps
refs.summary: Links can launch other programs → confirm in the shell, with an allowlist per link type → nothing launches silently.

refs.title: P4 task: Permission prompts
refs.summary: Camera, microphone, location, notifications and clipboard are sensitive → deny by default, allow per site, never stored inside WebView2 → you control access.

refs.title: P4 task: Safe downloads
refs.summary: Downloads can hide tricks → configured folder only, no auto-open, a warning for programs, cleaned file names → no folder-escape tricks.

refs.title: P4 task: Prove what is really isolated
refs.summary: Profiles share browser processes → test what is truly separate (cookies, storage, databases) and list what is shared → no claim of full isolation without evidence.

refs.title: P4 task: No app access for websites
refs.summary: Websites must not reach app internals → test every channel, including one internal command the permission system skips, and block loading the app's own pages → native access stays closed.

refs.title: P4 task: Security audit log
refs.summary: Denials need a record → one log line per denied action, old logs rolled over, with no page content → evidence without privacy leaks.

refs.title: P5 task: Export file format and run labels
refs.summary: Every later result is read from files → define one versioned format (plain data files) that labels each run with code version, Windows build, WebView2 version and settings → any number can be traced to the exact setup that made it.

refs.title: P5 task: Network log: coverage and cost
refs.summary: Some requests may be missed (embedded frames, redirects, background workers) → test each kind and run a small cost trial → the paper states exactly what the log covers.

refs.title: P5 task: Settings for measuring and logging
refs.summary: You decide what is recorded → add on/off switches for measurement and the network log, a button to open the log folder, and a retention limit → nothing is recorded that you did not choose.

refs.title: P5 task: Map tabs to browser processes
refs.summary: Tabs may share browser processes → check how each tab shows up and which processes serve it → P6 and P7 know how far per-tab numbers can be trusted.

refs.title: P5 task: Reading: measurement methods
refs.summary: Our methods must match good practice → read the literature on measurement and browser benchmarking → each headline measurement gets a final, cited definition.

refs.title: P5 task: Gate and your review
refs.summary: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the accuracy results and the privacy check and approve; only then does P6 start.

refs.title: P5 task: Count only Ferrum's own processes
refs.summary: Other apps on the PC also use WebView2 → find Ferrum's processes through Ferrum's own WebView2 setup, never by program name → other apps' memory never leaks into Ferrum's numbers.

refs.title: P5 task: Memory and CPU meter
refs.summary: We need trustworthy memory and CPU numbers → read them straight from Windows (private memory as the headline, working set as secondary, CPU time) and add them up over Ferrum's processes → one fair total per moment; peaks come from the total, never from adding per-process peaks.

refs.title: P5 task: Prove the meter is accurate
refs.summary: A meter is only useful if it is right → helper programs use a known amount of memory and CPU; the meter and an independent reader are compared with those values, with tolerances written down before the run → a meter that fails blocks P6.

refs.title: P5 task: Measure the meter's own cost
refs.summary: Measuring uses some CPU and memory itself → measure the meter's own cost at each sampling speed → we know how much it disturbs results (this describes the tool, not Ferrum).

refs.title: P5 task: Startup timing
refs.summary: Startup speed is a key result → record when the process starts, the window appears, and the first and largest content are drawn, read by Ferrum itself through the browser's debugging channel → startup can be compared fairly in P6.

refs.title: P5 task: Page-load timing
refs.summary: Page-load speed is another key result → record each load's main moments, whether it crossed to another site, and how many redirects it took → page loads can be compared fairly in P6.

refs.title: P5 task: Record tab state changes
refs.summary: Smart tab sleeping in P7 needs a record of every tab state change → define the record (from, to, why, when, which tab) and log hide and show now → P7 plugs in without a new format.

refs.title: P5 task: Network log: addresses and timings only
refs.summary: You asked for a log of network calls → per tab, save address, method, result, type, timing, size and the security decision to one folder per session, never headers or page content → useful for research without storing private data.

refs.title: P6 task: Bare Tauri app to compare against
refs.summary: We must show what Ferrum adds over plain Tauri → build a minimal app on the same Tauri and WebView2 versions with no Ferrum features → differences can be credited to Ferrum's design.

refs.title: P6 task: Statistics pipeline
refs.summary: Numbers need honest statistics → a Python pipeline computes averages, spread, confidence ranges, effect sizes and corrections for many comparisons, plus plots → the analysis is repeatable to the byte.

refs.title: P6 task: Measure the noise level
refs.summary: Some variation is just noise → run one product against itself (an A/A test) plus short pilots → we know the smallest real difference we can detect and set the trial count for each experiment.

refs.title: P6 task: Write predictions before testing
refs.summary: Deciding what counts as success after seeing data is biased → write each prediction and its meaningful-difference threshold first, and you approve them → results cannot be bent to fit.

refs.title: P6 task: First test campaign
refs.summary: The bench is ready and checked → run the footprint, startup, page-load, smoothness, reliability, security-cost and isolation-cost experiments (and energy if supported) on Chrome, Edge, bare Tauri and Ferrum without sleeping → raw data for P8 and a reference for P7.

refs.title: P6 task: Reproduction guides
refs.summary: Others must be able to repeat our tests → write how-to guides for benchmarking and for reproducing a campaign on a clean PC → the research can be checked independently.

refs.title: P6 task: Reading: benchmarking and statistics
refs.summary: Methods must follow good practice → read the literature on benchmark methods and performance statistics → the method pages cite it.

refs.title: P6 task: Gate and your review
refs.summary: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the first campaign and approve; only then does P7 start.

refs.title: P6 task: Ten local test workloads
refs.summary: Results must not depend on live websites → build ten local workloads (simple page, heavy web app, huge page, scrolling, many navigations, video, graphics, several active tabs, many background tabs, close and restore) → every product sees exactly the same content.

refs.title: P6 task: A few real websites as extras
refs.summary: Local pages may not reflect real use → pick a short list of public sites without login, with the visit date recorded → a reality check, clearly labelled extra, never the main result.

refs.title: P6 task: Fair settings for each product
refs.summary: Chrome and Edge have built-in resource savers → record every relevant setting per product in versioned files, never switching their savers off just to help Ferrum → the comparison is fair and anyone can check it.

refs.title: P6 task: Test runner
refs.summary: Trial order and leftovers can bias results → a Rust runner shuffles trials with a recorded seed, starts each product fresh with a clean profile, tracks all its processes, and records every trial including failures → runs are fair, resumable and complete.

refs.title: P6 task: Scripts that drive each workload
refs.summary: Each product must be driven the same way → one browser-automation script (Playwright) per workload, connecting to every product through the same debugging channel → differences come from the products, not the driver.

refs.title: P6 task: Record the setup and pin versions
refs.summary: A silent browser update mid-campaign would spoil the data → record Windows build, product versions, power plan and background apps for each run, and pin browser versions → any change is caught and flagged.

refs.title: P6 task: Smoothness measurement
refs.summary: Smooth scrolling and animation matter to users → measure frame timing with a Windows tool (PresentMon) and long-frame data inside the page → smoothness can be compared, or marked unsupported for a product.

refs.title: P6 task: Energy, only if it can be measured honestly
refs.summary: Energy use is worth reporting but hard to measure → if you approve, a separate admin-level reader collects CPU energy counters (labelled modelled, CPU only), or a wall-power meter is used → otherwise energy is marked unsupported, never estimated.

refs.title: P7 task: Tab state machine
refs.summary: Each tab must always be in one clear state (active, background, idle, close candidate, closed, restoring) → write the allowed moves as a fixed table with tests → the tab you are using can never be closed by mistake.

refs.title: P7 task: Write predictions before testing
refs.summary: Deciding what counts as success after seeing data is biased → write each prediction and its meaningful-difference threshold first, and you approve them → results cannot be bent to fit.

refs.title: P7 task: Strategy campaign
refs.summary: Bench and predictions are ready → run the four strategies on identical workloads, with Chrome and Edge as shipped for reference → raw data for P8.

refs.title: P7 task: Literature check: what is really new
refs.summary: Similar ideas exist (Chrome and Edge tab sleeping, Android app standby, cost-aware caching) → compare our approach with each, using verified sources, and you approve the assessment → the paper claims only what is truly new.

refs.title: P7 task: Gate and your review
refs.summary: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review and approve; only then does P8 start.

refs.title: P7 task: Optional rerun with smart sleeping
refs.summary: The first campaign tested Ferrum without sleeping → if you pick option (a) in [this open question](ref:Q-208), rerun footprint, page-load, smoothness, energy and reliability with smart sleeping, same rules, kept separate → otherwise the gap is recorded as a known limitation.

refs.title: P7 task: Signals for sleep decisions
refs.summary: Good decisions need inputs → measure last use, memory pressure, tab activity, cost to restore, media playing, downloads, your exclusions and unsaved forms → each strategy decides on real signals with known limits.

refs.title: P7 task: Sleep actions: hide, suspend, close, restore
refs.summary: Sleeping has levels → build hide, suspend, low-memory mode and close-but-remember (address, history, scroll position), plus restore → each strategy can pick the right level.

refs.title: P7 task: Safety guards
refs.summary: Closing a tab mid-task can lose your work → never close a tab while media plays, a download runs, a form is unsaved, the page asks before leaving, or you excluded the site → sleeping never costs you data.

refs.title: P7 task: Three simple strategies
refs.summary: We need baselines to compare against → build never sleep, sleep after a fixed idle time, and sleep under memory pressure, switchable by a setting → one app runs every strategy, so only the strategy differs.

refs.title: P7 task: Cost-aware strategy
refs.summary: Smarter choices weigh memory saved, energy and restore delay → combine them in one weighted score (energy weight zero if energy cannot be measured) and fix the weights on separate calibration workloads → the strategy is not tuned to the test it is judged on.

refs.title: P7 task: Log every sleep decision
refs.summary: We must see what each strategy did → record every state change and refusal, and the time from restore to first content → behaviour and restore delay become measurable.

refs.title: P7 task: Long-running test
refs.summary: Some problems only show up over hours → run many background tabs for a long session under each strategy, watching memory growth, crashes and restores → every bug found is fixed, with a test, before the campaign.

refs.title: P7 task: Bench settings for each strategy
refs.summary: The test bench needs a setup per strategy → add one settings file for each Ferrum strategy → the only difference between Ferrum runs is the strategy switch.

refs.title: P8 task: Set up the paper project
refs.summary: We need a paper that builds from day one → set up the LaTeX project with the [proposed ACM template](ref:adr-0017); Claude installs the tools and you click the admin prompt ([who installs](ref:adr-0021)) → writing can start any time.

refs.title: P8 task: Reproducibility package
refs.summary: Others must be able to check our work → package the guide, scripts, setup records and data (or an archive with checksums) with a data licence → anyone can rebuild every figure.

refs.title: P8 task: AI-use statement
refs.summary: Venues require disclosure of AI help → finish the AI-use statement to match the chosen venue's policy, with the human authors' responsibility → honest and compliant.

refs.title: P8 task: Integrity check and your review
refs.summary: The paper is drafted → a checklist confirms no invented facts, versions, measurements, citations or novelty → you read the paper and approve the end of P8.

refs.title: P8 task: Analyse the campaigns
refs.summary: Raw data alone proves nothing → run the statistics pipeline on all campaign data and mark each prediction supported, not supported or inconclusive → every verdict links to its analysis.

refs.title: P8 task: Figures and numbers from scripts only
refs.summary: Hand-typed numbers invite mistakes → every figure, table and number in the paper is generated by a script, with a record of which data made each → every number is traceable.

refs.title: P8 task: Trace from question to conclusion
refs.summary: Each conclusion must rest on evidence → build a table linking each question to its prediction, experiment, raw data, analysis, figure and conclusion, shown in this portal → gaps are visible at a glance.

refs.title: P8 task: Write method and design sections
refs.summary: Method and design do not depend on results → write method, architecture, tab-sleeping design and background first → the paper moves on without waiting for data.

refs.title: P8 task: Write results and limitations
refs.summary: Results must come only from finished analysis → after it, write results, security and usability trade-offs, and the limits (energy, process counting, debugging-channel effects, one PC) → no early or unsupported claims.

refs.title: P8 task: Related work, introduction, abstract
refs.summary: Claims of novelty must match the approved literature check → write related work from it, then the introduction and abstract last → the paper never overclaims.

refs.title: P8 task: Verify every citation
refs.summary: A wrong citation damages trust → a script confirms each reference against its source or its permanent paper ID (DOI) → no unverified or banned references.

refs.title: P8 task: Report failed experiments too
refs.summary: Hiding failures is cherry-picking → list every failed or stopped run from the log and run records in the paper or its appendix → the record is honest.

refs.title: Decision 1: Plan first, then build phase by phase with your sign-off
refs.summary: Nine phases, P0 to P8. P0 is planning only, with no app code. A phase starts when you approve its plan and ends when its tests pass and you approve the result. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 2: The wiki is Claude's working memory
refs.summary: Claude keeps plans, decisions and research as linked pages in the wiki (Karpathy's 'LLM wiki' pattern). Your raw notes are never edited; Claude maintains everything else. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 3: Work survives interrupted sessions
refs.summary: After every task Claude updates the status page and the log. When a session ends it writes a handoff note, and the next session reads them and carries on. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 4: A usable app and solid research, equally
refs.summary: Each phase delivers something usable plus the measurement hooks the research needs. The app is never tuned just to win a benchmark. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 5: You install the developer tools (replaced)
refs.summary: You would run the install commands Claude supplied; Claude would only check the versions afterwards. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 6: Browser controls in plain TypeScript, no UI framework
refs.summary: Tab bar and address bar are plain TypeScript bundled by Vite. The controls never draw over the web page area. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 7: One window, many web views
refs.summary: A trusted panel draws Ferrum's controls; each website tab is its own untrusted web view in the same window. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 8: Network log records what was fetched, never the content
refs.summary: For each request Ferrum logs address, method, status, type, timing, size, tab and block decision, one line per request in a file. No headers, no page content. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 9: Benchmarks run on your AMD desktop
refs.summary: All measurements run on this machine. Energy is reported only as the CPU chip's own estimate, clearly labelled; whole-system energy only with a wall meter; per-program energy never. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 10: Sites kept apart by profiles in one shared browser process
refs.summary: Each site gets its own WebView2 profile (own cookies and storage) while all share one browser process. How to build it is still open and must be settled before P3. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 11: Git, GitHub checks, open licence; only you upload
refs.summary: Code lives in git. Automatic checks run on GitHub's Windows machines. Licence: MIT or Apache 2.0. Claude never pushes; you create the GitHub repo and push. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 12: Benchmark robot: Rust controller plus Playwright scripts
refs.summary: A Rust program schedules trials and measures memory and CPU through Windows. Playwright scripts in TypeScript drive the pages. Every browser is driven the same way. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 13: Statistics in Python scripts
refs.summary: Analysis runs as repeatable Python scripts, not notebooks. Each comparison reports averages, spread, confidence ranges and effect sizes, with recorded random seeds. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 14: You review the result of every phase
refs.summary: At the end of every phase, planning included, Claude runs the tests, saves the output, writes a short report and stops. The next phase starts only after you approve the phase and then explicitly say go. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 15: Open browsing with a blocklist
refs.summary: Any secure (HTTPS) site opens unless blocked. Plain HTTP is upgraded or warned about. Other link types (mail, apps) ask first. Local files and address-bar scripts are refused in tabs. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 16: Plan app reads the wiki and takes approvals (replaced)
refs.summary: A local Next.js app would show the wiki pages, and you would click Approve there. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 17: Research paper in the ACM LaTeX template, for now
refs.summary: The paper uses ACM's acmart template until a venue is chosen. Text stays portable, and no results section is written until experiments are done. Claude proposed; open to your veto.

refs.title: Decision 18: Repo folder is the project folder; Rust code in one workspace
refs.summary: The planned folder layout (app, libraries, benchmarks, analysis, paper) sits directly at the repo root, plus folders for the baseline app, the benchmark robot and the throwaway test builds (kept as evidence). You approved it on 11 Oct. Claude proposed; you approved.

refs.title: Decision 19: Unsafe WebView2 code lives in one audited module
refs.summary: Features Tauri lacks (sleep, memory target, network events, crash detection) use raw WebView2 calls, all in one module behind a safe Rust interface. Two small Windows modules for measuring memory and CPU may also use unsafe code, each with its own safety notes. You approved it on 11 Oct. Claude proposed; you approved.

refs.title: Decision 20: Wiki index lists evidence folders, not every file
refs.summary: The wiki index names each evidence folder once instead of every file in it. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 21: Claude runs all tool installs
refs.summary: Claude runs the install commands, including ones that need admin rights (you click through the Windows prompts), and records exact versions. Kernel drivers still need your separate approval. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 22: A broken approvals file stops the wiki check
refs.summary: If the approvals file is unreadable or approves a missing page, the wiki check now fails instead of only warning. A decision you rejected is also flagged. Claude proposed; open to your veto.

refs.title: Decision 23: You approve in Claude Code; the portal is read-only
refs.summary: You say what you approve in Claude Code. Claude saves your words, then records the approval with a fingerprint of the page. If the page changes later, Claude asks again. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 24: The portal shows only plain-language JSON
refs.summary: Whenever Claude edits the wiki, it rewrites the matching plain-language JSON in the same step. The portal reads only that JSON, never the wiki; it also shows, read-only, the check scripts that JSON names. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 25: Check scripts in PowerShell 7
refs.summary: Every task gets one script that proves it is done, and every phase one gate script that runs all its checks. Each part is commented in plain words. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 26: Architecture in four groups
refs.summary: Components are shown as Application, Benchmark, Testing and quality, and Research and analysis, led by a layered picture of the Rust app. You decided.

refs.title: Decision 27: Mask private network and machine details
refs.summary: Real IP addresses, machine names, network card ids and your user-folder path are replaced by placeholders. Real values stay in one local file that git ignores. You decided.

refs.title: Tauri cannot yet give each site its own profile
refs.summary: Sites are to be kept apart by separate WebView2 profiles, but a profile can only be set when a web view is created, and Tauri does not pass it through yet.

refs.title: Multi-view feature may be unstable
refs.summary: Many web views in one window needs a Tauri feature marked experimental. Known bugs: hangs, blank views, lost keyboard focus.

refs.title: Tab sleep and memory saving need unsafe low-level code
refs.summary: The WebView2 calls that put a tab to sleep or ask it to use less memory are not in Tauri, so we must reach them through unsafe code. Sleep can also simply fail.

refs.title: AMD energy readings may be estimates
refs.summary: Research suggests AMD's energy counters are modelled rather than measured, cover only the CPU chip, and need admin rights plus a kernel driver.

refs.title: Counting each browser's memory fairly is hard
refs.summary: Browsers run many helper processes, some shared. Counting the wrong ones, or double-counting shared memory, would make the main comparison wrong.

refs.title: The test robot sees WebView2 less clearly
refs.summary: Playwright reaches WebView2 only through a debugging channel it calls lower fidelity, and an open channel may itself change behaviour.

refs.title: Navigation filter could let blocked pages through
refs.summary: Tauri's navigation check allows any address it cannot read, and never sees pages loaded inside frames, so a blocked site could slip in.

refs.title: Network log needs low-level code
refs.summary: Tauri has no hook that sees normal web traffic, so the network log must use unsafe WebView2 calls, or the debugging channel as a fallback.

refs.title: All web views must share identical start-up settings
refs.summary: Web views sharing one data folder must use exactly the same settings (flags, proxy, language) or creation fails, so no per-tab differences.

refs.title: Google sign-in will refuse Ferrum tabs
refs.summary: Google's rules block sign-in from embedded web views like Ferrum's tabs, so Google login is expected to fail.

refs.title: Browsers update themselves mid-study
refs.summary: Chrome, Edge and WebView2 update automatically. A version change during a measurement run makes the results incomparable.

refs.title: Windows background work and heat add noise
refs.summary: Updates, antivirus, indexing, CPU temperature and even window visibility change the numbers, adding noise or bias.

refs.title: Rivals' power-saving features can skew comparisons
refs.summary: Edge and Chrome ship sleeping tabs, Startup Boost and Memory Saver. On or off changes who wins, and switching them off just to help Ferrum is not allowed.

refs.title: Our own tools could bias the results
refs.summary: The team building Ferrum also builds the benchmark, so bias can creep in through tooling or through choices made after seeing data.

refs.title: A session can stop mid-change and lose state
refs.summary: Sessions run out of tokens. A stop in the middle of a multi-file change can leave broken work or a wrong status page.

refs.title: Scope creep: two equal goals, no tie-breaker
refs.summary: The app and the research weigh the same and both wish lists are long, so work can grow without anyone deciding it should.

refs.title: Our tab-sleep policy may not be new
refs.summary: Chrome, Edge, ChromeOS and Android already freeze, sleep or discard tabs. Claiming novelty without a proper literature review would be wrong.

refs.title: Bugs in unsafe low-level code
refs.summary: Several features need unsafe Windows code. Mistakes there can crash Ferrum, leak memory, or keep closed tabs alive.

refs.title: A change could expose Ferrum's internals to websites
refs.summary: Every web view can technically message Ferrum's Rust code. A configuration slip could let a website run privileged commands or weaken isolation.

refs.title: Tools and libraries change under us
refs.summary: Over months, Tauri, Node, TypeScript, ESLint and Mermaid release new major versions that can break the build.

refs.title: One machine may not speak for all
refs.summary: All results come from one AMD desktop. Memory and process behaviour depend on the machine, so results may not hold elsewhere.

refs.title: Approval records could be wrong
refs.summary: Phases start only when approvals match the current pages. A fingerprint bug, a corrupt file, or an approval you never gave would start or block work wrongly.

refs.title: Sleeping or closing a tab could lose your work
refs.summary: If Ferrum sleeps or discards a tab during a download, a call, or while you are typing, data could be lost.

refs.title: Your reviews can become a bottleneck
refs.summary: Every phase waits for your approval, and any edit to an approved page needs re-approval. Reviews piling up can stall work.

refs.title: Too few trials to see real differences
refs.summary: With about 30 trials per setup only fairly large differences are detectable; small but meaningful ones could be missed.

refs.title: Memory and CPU versus browsers
refs.summary: Does Ferrum, with no tab sleeping, use less memory and CPU than Chrome, Edge and a bare-bones Tauri app on the same test pages? We count only the processes each product starts itself, so nothing is missed or counted twice.

refs.title: Speed: startup, page loads, smoothness
refs.summary: Does showing websites inside Ferrum make startup, page loads or scrolling slower than in Chrome, Edge or the bare-bones app? Ferrum puts each tab in its own embedded web view and checks every navigation, which could add delay.

refs.title: Energy use
refs.summary: Can we measure energy honestly on this AMD desktop and, if so, does Ferrum use less energy per task than Chrome and Edge? The AMD chip's energy counter is a model, not a meter. If it fails our checks, energy is reported as not measurable, never guessed.

refs.title: Smart tab sleeping (the central question)
refs.summary: Does a smart tab-sleeping policy balance memory, energy and tab wake-up time better than no sleeping or a simple timer, without ever unloading a tab it must keep? Tab sleeping means pausing or unloading tabs you are not using. Scored with the overall score J. Similar ideas exist, so nothing is claimed as new before the literature review.

refs.title: Cost of the security checks
refs.summary: How much delay and memory do Ferrum's site-blocking and permission checks add, compared with the same build with the checks switched off? The checks-off build exists only for this test and is never shipped. Whether the checks work is tested separately.

refs.title: Cost of keeping sites apart
refs.summary: With one WebView2 profile per site, what is still shared, and how much extra memory and processes does it cost versus the alternatives? Alternatives: one shared profile, or one data folder per site. We must list exactly what stays shared. It depends on per-site profiles working in Ferrum (an open risk).

refs.title: Reliability over long use
refs.summary: Does Ferrum stay as stable as Chrome and Edge over hours of use, and does it restore sessions and recover from tab crashes and network drops? Covers memory creep over long runs, crashes, crash recovery and session restore.

refs.title: Ferrum uses less memory than Chrome and Edge
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum (no tab sleeping) to use less memory than Chrome and Edge as shipped, on an idle page and on 4 active tabs; we would be wrong if its typical use is equal or higher.

refs.title: Ferrum adds little on top of a bare-bones Tauri app
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum's idle memory to be less than 20% above a bare-bones Tauri app showing the same page; we would be wrong if the extra could be 20% or more.

refs.title: Without tab sleeping, Ferrum burns more background CPU
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum without tab sleeping to use more CPU per minute on 20 background tabs than Chrome and Edge; we would be wrong if it uses the same or less.

refs.title: Ferrum opens its window faster
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum's first window to appear sooner than Chrome's and Edge's on a fresh start; we would be wrong if it is the same or slower.

refs.title: Page loads are not slower
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum's page-load time to stay within 10% of Chrome and Edge for every kind of navigation; we would be wrong if it is 10% or more slower for any one kind.

refs.title: Scrolling and animation are as smooth
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum's frame timing and missed frames while scrolling and animating to stay within the margins of Chrome and Edge; we would be wrong if either is worse by the margin or more.

refs.title: Ferrum uses less energy per task (if measurable)
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum to use less energy than Chrome and Edge for an idle page and for video playback; we would be wrong if it uses the same or more.

refs.title: Smart sleeping saves memory
refs.summary: We expect the smart policy to use less memory on 20 background tabs than no sleeping; we would be wrong if memory is the same or higher.

refs.title: Smart sleeping gets the best overall score
refs.summary: We expect the smart policy to get the lowest score J on both tab-sleeping workloads, and to win for at least two thirds of weight choices; we would be wrong if a simpler policy ties or beats it.

refs.title: Smart sleeping wakes tabs faster than a timer
refs.summary: We expect the slowest 5% of tab wake-ups to be faster under the smart policy than under the fixed timer; we would be wrong if they are the same or slower.

refs.title: No policy ever unloads a protected tab
refs.summary: We expect zero cases of a tab being unloaded while it plays media, downloads, holds an unsaved form or is excluded by you; we would be wrong if even one happens.

refs.title: Security checks cost almost nothing
refs.summary: We expect each security decision to take under 1 ms (95% of the time), and page loads and memory to be at most 5% above a checks-off build; we would be wrong if any limit is broken.

refs.title: Per-site profiles are cheaper than per-site data folders
refs.summary: We expect each extra site to add less memory with one profile per site than with one data folder per site; we would be wrong if it adds the same or more.

refs.title: Memory does not creep up over long sessions
refs.summary: We expect Ferrum's memory growth during a long browsing run to be within 10 MiB per hour of Chrome and Edge; we would be wrong if it grows that much faster or more.

refs.title: Sessions restore and crashes recover
refs.summary: We expect at least 95% of sessions to restore correctly (cautious end of the range) and every forced tab crash to recover in time; we would be wrong if either fails.

refs.title: Memory and CPU footprint
refs.summary: Run: idle page, JavaScript app, huge page, 4 active tabs, 20 background tabs, a few public sites; 30+ rounds in random order. Compare: Chrome, Edge, bare-bones Tauri app, Ferrum with and without tab sleeping (savers-off Chrome and Edge only as a side analysis). Measure: private memory, process count, CPU time.

refs.title: Energy per task
refs.summary: Run: first check the energy reading is trustworthy (if not: report 'not measurable' and stop); then idle page, video, JavaScript app, background tabs. Compare: the five products. Measure: energy per task above idle.

refs.title: Cost of keeping sites apart
refs.summary: Run: active tabs on 1, 2, 4 and 8 sites. Compare: one shared profile, one profile per site, one data folder per site. Measure: extra memory and processes per site, plus a list of what stays shared.

refs.title: Tab-sleeping policies compared
refs.summary: Run: 20 background tabs with scripted tab switches, open-close-restore cycles, active tabs, video; tune the smart policy on separate data first. Compare: Ferrum with no sleeping, timer, memory-pressure and smart policies; Chrome and Edge as reference only. Measure: memory, energy, wake-up time, score J, safety violations.

refs.title: Page-load speed
refs.summary: Run: 200 link clicks across seven kinds of navigation, plus a few public sites. Compare: Chrome, Edge, bare-bones Tauri app, Ferrum with and without tab sleeping. Measure: page-load time and failed loads.

refs.title: Reliability, long runs and recovery
refs.summary: Run: 2-hour browsing runs (10 per product), restart-and-restore cycles, forced tab crashes, test-server outages. Compare: the five products (restore only where it can be scripted the same way). Measure: memory growth, crashes, recovery time, restore success.

refs.title: Smoothness of scrolling and animation
refs.summary: Run: scrolling a long page, canvas and 3D animation, a huge page, a JavaScript app. Compare: the same five products. Measure: time between frames, missed frames, long blocking frames, animation work per second.

refs.title: Cost of the security checks
refs.summary: Run: 300 mixed navigations, some to blocked sites, all local. Compare: normal Ferrum versus a test-only build with the checks off. Measure: time per security decision, page-load time (allowed pages only), memory.

refs.title: Startup speed
refs.summary: Run: launch each product to a simple page, fresh and warm starts, 30 times each. Compare: Chrome, Edge, bare-bones Tauri app, Ferrum. Measure: time to first window, first content and main content.

refs.title: Animation work rate
refs.summary: Fixed units of drawing work the canvas or 3D test page completes per second. Unit: ops/s.

refs.title: Chip energy estimate (AMD)
refs.summary: Energy the AMD processor reports for itself. It is a model, leaves out memory chips and is not a wall reading, so it is labelled an estimate. Used only if it passes its checks. Unit: J.

refs.title: Crashes
refs.summary: Crashed or frozen page, graphics or main processes, per run and per hour. Unit: count per hour.

refs.title: Time between frames
refs.summary: The gap between frames shown on screen while scrolling or animating. We look at the slow end (the slowest 5%). Unit: ms.

refs.title: Missed frames
refs.summary: Share of screen refreshes where a new frame was due but none appeared. Unit: share (0-1).

refs.title: Tab state changes
refs.summary: How often tabs move between states such as idle, unloaded, waking and active. Unit: count.

refs.title: Time the page was too busy
refs.summary: Time per minute the page could not respond because a frame took too long, from the browser's own long-frame reports. Unit: ms per minute.

refs.title: Memory growth over time
refs.summary: How fast private memory climbs during a long run, using a trend fit that ignores outliers. Unit: MiB/h.

refs.title: Failed page loads
refs.summary: Failed navigations divided by attempted ones. A load fails if the page does not report back in time or the product shows an error. Unit: share (0-1).

refs.title: Page-load time
refs.summary: From starting a navigation to the new page finishing its load, as the page itself reports it. Unit: ms.

refs.title: Overall score J
refs.summary: J adds up memory, energy and tab wake-up time, each divided by Ferrum's value with no tab sleeping, so 'no sleeping' scores 1 and lower is better. Weights are fixed before the real runs (equal thirds proposed; if energy is not measurable it is dropped), and we show how results change across 66 other weightings.

refs.title: Peak private memory
refs.summary: The highest private memory reached during the test. Unit: MiB.

refs.title: Time per security decision
refs.summary: How long Ferrum takes to decide allow, block or ask for one navigation or permission request (not counting your answer). Unit: µs.

refs.title: Number of processes
refs.summary: How many processes the product runs, split by kind (main, page, graphics, helper). Unit: count.

refs.title: Crash recovery time
refs.summary: From a forced tab crash until the tab's page is ready again. Unit: ms.

refs.title: Tab wake-up time
refs.summary: From switching to a background tab until its page is ready again, including a full reload if the tab was unloaded. Unit: ms.

refs.title: Session restore success
refs.summary: Share of tabs brought back correctly (address, scroll position and page state) after a restart or after being unloaded. Unit: share (0-1).

refs.title: Safety violations
refs.summary: Times a policy unloaded or paused a tab it had to protect (playing media, download, unsaved form, your exclusion and similar). Target: zero. Unit: count.

refs.title: Time to first content
refs.summary: From launch to the start page showing its first text or image. Unit: ms.

refs.title: Time to main content
refs.summary: From launch to the start page showing its largest element. With first content and busy time, it replaces the retired 'time to interactive'. Unit: ms.

refs.title: Time to first window
refs.summary: From launching the program to its first window appearing. Unit: ms.

refs.title: CPU cycles
refs.summary: Processor work counted in clock cycles. Reported next to CPU time because it reacts differently when the clock speed changes. Unit: cycles.

refs.title: CPU time
refs.summary: Processor time used by all of the product's processes, per task, or per minute while tabs sit in the background. Unit: s.

refs.title: Private memory (main memory measure)
refs.summary: Memory reserved only for this product, added up over every process it started and averaged over the test. Shared pages are not counted twice. Not checked yet (P5). Unit: MiB.

refs.title: Private memory held in RAM
refs.summary: The part of private memory that sits in RAM. A secondary measure. Unit: MiB.

refs.title: All memory in RAM (over-counts)
refs.summary: All memory in RAM, but pages shared by several processes are counted once per process. Shown only with that warning. Unit: MiB.

refs.title: Wall-socket energy
refs.summary: Energy from a plug-in logging power meter, minus idle energy. Used only if such a meter is available. Unit: J.

refs.title: Canvas and 3D animation
refs.summary: One minute of 2D canvas and one minute of WebGL (3D) drawing, with fixed scenes. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Continuous scrolling
refs.summary: A very long page that scrolls itself at a fixed speed for 60 seconds, the same in every product. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Many page loads
refs.summary: 200 navigations across seven kinds (same site, other site, redirects, back/forward, cached, uncached). A 2-hour repeat is used for reliability. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Very large page
refs.summary: A page with 100,000 elements and 2,000 style rules; scripted clicks force it to re-lay itself out. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Many background tabs
refs.summary: 1 front tab and 20 background tabs (some playing media, holding an unsaved form or a download) for 30 minutes, with 40 scripted tab switches. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Several active tabs
refs.summary: 4 busy tabs on 4 sites, switching the front tab every 10 seconds for 5 minutes. The isolation test varies the number of sites. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: A few public websites
refs.summary: Real public sites (list needs your approval), one visit each, no login. Reported separately, never mixed with the local tests. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Mix of allowed and blocked links
refs.summary: 300 local navigations: 20% to blocked sites and 10% redirects to blocked sites. Used only to measure the cost of the security checks. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Open, close and restore
refs.summary: 50 cycles of opening 5 tabs, unloading or closing them and restoring them; the app restarts every 10 cycles. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: JavaScript-heavy web app
refs.summary: A local app that switches views 20 times, each drawing a 5,000-item list and running fixed computations. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Simple article page
refs.summary: A local page with text and 10 images, no scripts. Used for idle tests and as the startup page. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Video playback
refs.summary: A home-made 1080p, 30 fps test video played for 2 minutes. No third-party content. Settings are proposed; the test page is built in P6.

refs.title: Browser controls
refs.summary: The window you use: tabs on top, address bar, back, forward, reload, settings and a Ferrum panel on the right ([the look you chose](ref:adr-0028)). Our code: a TypeScript screen plus a Rust host that wires the engine parts together. Risk: the multi-view feature it needs is experimental in Tauri; not checked yet (checked in P1).

refs.title: Plain Tauri app (comparison point)
refs.summary: The simplest Tauri app that shows one web page, with no Ferrum features. Trusted; not shipped. Comparing with it separates Ferrum's own cost or savings from the cost of Tauri and WebView2.

refs.title: Benchmark harness
refs.summary: Starts each browser fresh, runs the same scripted workloads many times in random order, and measures from outside so every browser is measured the same way. Trusted; not shipped. Risk: proving Ferrum's helper processes are counted fairly; not checked yet (checked in P6).

refs.title: Chrome and Edge
refs.summary: The browsers Ferrum is compared with. Not ours. Run with their normal resource-saving features on, never switched off to favour Ferrum; their settings are recorded in every trial.

refs.title: Core library
refs.summary: The shared base every Rust part uses: settings with defaults and checks, ids and record formats. Trusted. It calls nothing itself; everything else depends on it.

refs.title: Plan portal (this site)
refs.summary: The site you are reading. A planning tool, not part of Ferrum: a read-only portal with seven tabs that shows Claude's plain-language text and each check script. You start it with one PowerShell script and approve things in Claude Code.

refs.title: Measurement: network log
refs.summary: Writes every tab's network calls to a folder you can review: address, status, timing and size. Never headers, cookies or page content. Trusted. Its cost in speed and memory is not measured yet (measured in P5).

refs.title: Statistics and figures
refs.summary: Python scripts that turn archived raw results into statistics, charts and reports for the paper. Trusted; not shipped. They read only archived runs, so every figure traces back to its data.

refs.title: Tab sleeping
refs.summary: Watches idle tabs and memory, then hides, pauses or unloads idle tabs and restores them when needed. Trusted. Four policies to compare: none, fixed idle time, memory pressure, adaptive. Never unloads the tab you are using. Risk: unloading could lose what you typed. Before P7, background tabs are only hidden.

refs.title: Security policy
refs.summary: Decides what is allowed: sites, pop-ups, downloads, permissions and links to other apps. Trusted. Refuses when unsure and logs every refusal. Pure rules with no browser inside, so each rule can be tested on its own. Basic rules in P2, the full engine in P4.

refs.title: Websites in tabs
refs.summary: Any website you open, each in its own view. Untrusted: treated as the attacker and sandboxed. Its view is created by Ferrum, so it should have no bridge to the app at all (checked in P2); if one appeared, every command would be refused.

refs.title: Measurement: memory, CPU and timings
refs.summary: Inside the app: records memory and CPU of Ferrum's processes, startup and page timings, and every tab sleep or wake, then exports data files. Trusted. A cross-check only: the official cross-browser numbers come from the benchmark harness. Risk: counting exactly the right processes.

refs.title: Tab & view manager
refs.summary: Creates, shows, hides and closes each website view; handles navigation, sessions and downloads. Trusted.
